patches.old: This is the most common question type in CARS, and it is where the most points are won and lost.
patches.new: Inference questions are among the most frequently encountered in CARS, and they are where many points are won and lost.
patches.reason: The AAMC publishes percentages only for its three skill categories, not for individual question types, so 'the most common question type' is not a supportable claim.

patches.old: Speed matters because on test day you have approximately 90 seconds per question total, and spending 15 seconds figuring out what a question is asking is a significant tax.
patches.new: Speed matters because on test day the section averages about 100 seconds per question (90 minutes across 53 questions), and much of that goes to reading the passage — so spending 15 seconds working out what a question is asking is a significant tax.
patches.reason: 90 minutes over 53 questions is about 1 minute 42 seconds, not 90 seconds.

patches.old: Avoiding these three errors alone can recover four to six points on a CARS section.
patches.new: Avoiding these three errors removes a whole class of avoidable misses — ones where the reading was fine and only the task was misread.
patches.reason: The four-to-six point figure is not supported by any published data; on the 118–132 CARS scale it would be an implausibly large effect.

visual.title: Stem language by question type
visual.alt: A table of seven question types, each with its giveaway stem phrases, the real task, and the classic wrong answer. Main idea: primary purpose, mainly concerned with, best title; characterize the whole passage; wrong answers are too specific, too broad, or the wrong tone. Detail or retrieval: according to, the author states, indicates; locate what is explicitly written; wrong answers are true in the world but never stated. Inference: it can be inferred, implies, suggests, would agree; extend the logic exactly one step; wrong answers are too extreme or speculative. Function: primarily in order to, serves to, the function of; name the rhetorical move; the wrong answer summarizes content instead of function. Strengthen or weaken: if true, would support, would undermine; judge new information against a specific claim; wrong answers run the opposite direction or are merely on-topic. Application: most analogous, suppose, how would the author respond; match the principle, not the surface; the wrong answer shares surface features with different logic. Vocabulary in context: as used in, in the context of, most nearly means; find the contextual meaning; the trap is the common dictionary definition. A footer names three costly category errors.
visual.caption: The first few words of the stem usually settle the question type.
